lead: Push a long rod from its ends and it may not crush; it bows sideways and fails suddenly. That is buckling. Any member in axial compression is a strut; a vertical one is a column. Its safe load depends on its length, its section, and how its ends are held. Columns appear in building frames, press rams, truss members and scissor lifts. This chapter sorts compression members by how they fail and by their end conditions, so later formulas use the right ideal case.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for stress, strain and factor of safety, and Unit 4 for centroid and second moment of area; Euler's formula itself is in 7.2.

blocks.text: A member that carries an axial push is a compression member. If it lies at any angle, as in a roof truss, it is a strut. If it stands vertical, as a building column or a press ram, it is a column. Some syllabi use the two words for the same member. The direction on the drawing does not change the physics; the push does.

Compression members are classed by how they fail. A short column, with small length to least radius of gyration L/r, fails by crushing: the material reaches its compressive strength. A long column, with large L/r, bends sideways and fails by buckling at a load far below the crushing load. An intermediate column fails by a mixture: yielding and bending happen together. The dividing lines are not fixed numbers; they come from the material and the end conditions.

Why does sideways bending win? A real member has a small initial curve or a load not exactly on the axis. The push then has a small lever arm. Bending grows the deflection, and the deflection grows the bending. At a critical load the growth runs away. That load is the buckling load, also called the crippling load or Euler load. It is a stability limit, not a strength limit.
The same steel rod can be a tie in one bay and a strut in another. A tie is pulled and cannot buckle. A strut is pushed and must be checked for buckling.
The load at which a column buckles depends on how its ends are held. A held end can stop translation, rotation or both. The five ideal cases used in textbooks are:

items: Both ends pinned (hinged): the ends cannot move sideways but can rotate; the column bows in one curve.
Both ends fixed: the ends cannot move or rotate; the column bows in an S shape.
One end fixed, one end free: a flagpole; the free top can move and rotate.
One end fixed, one end pinned: a clamp at the base and a hinge at the top.
Both ends fixed but free to move sideways: the ends keep their slope but the whole column sways.

blocks.text: An end that can rotate lets the column bow early. An end that is clamped forces a point of inflection and makes the column behave as if it were shorter. A free end adds a swaying cantilever action, the weakest case.
Each case replaces L by an effective length Le. L is the actual length between supports, in metres. The values of Le are in 7.3; the derivation of Euler's load is in 7.2.

sections.h3: Area, least I and radius of gyration

blocks.text: For buckling, three section properties matter. A is the area in m². I is the second moment of area about the axis of bending, in m⁴. r is the radius of gyration, in metres. The ratio Le/r is the slenderness ratio; 7.3 uses it.

blocks.where: r is the least radius of gyration in metres (m); I is the least second moment of area in m⁴; A is the cross-section area in m².

blocks.text: A section has many centroidal axes. Buckling takes the path of least resistance, so the smallest I controls. Call it I_min; its radius is r_min. For an I-section the weak axis is usually the one through the web. A flat ruler bends easily about its thin edge, not its broad face.

Do not use the strong axis just because it gives a bigger load. A column can bend sideways in any direction, so it chooses the softest direction first. Built-up sections need checking about both axes, and the smaller r governs.

Euler's crippling load, critical load and buckling load mean the same thing: the axial push at which the straight form becomes unstable. It is not the crushing load. The Euler expression and its limits are in 7.2 and 7.3.

examples.question: A steel rod of diameter d = 30 mm and length 2.0 m is used (a) as a tie rod in a roof truss and (b) as a vertical strut carrying a compressive load. Find its area, least second moment of area and least radius of gyration. State which use needs a buckling check.
steps: Convert d = 30 mm = 0.030 m. The length is L = 2.0 m.
Second moment I = π d⁴/64 = π(0.030)⁴/64 = 3.976 × 10⁻⁸ m⁴. For a solid round rod every centroidal axis has this same value, so it is the least I.
The tie is in tension; tension pulls the rod straight and cannot buckle. The strut is in compression; it can buckle about any axis, so it needs a buckling check with L and r.
examples.answer: A = 7.069 × 10⁻⁴ m², I = 3.976 × 10⁻⁸ m⁴, r = 7.5 mm; the strut needs the buckling check, the tie does not.
examples.check:
import math
d = 30e-3
A = math.pi * d**2 / 4
I = math.pi * d**4 / 64
r = math.sqrt(I / A)
print(f"{A:.3e}")
print(f"{I:.3e}")
print(f"{r:.4f}")
print(f"{r*1000:.1f}")

traps: Using the strong axis. A column bends about the axis with the smallest I, so always take I_min and r_min.
Treating the Euler load as a crushing strength. It is a stability limit and is valid only while the stress stays below the proportional limit; see 7.3.
Confusing actual length L with effective length Le. The end conditions replace L by Le before Euler's formula is used.
Calling every compression member a column. A strut may lie at any angle; a column is vertical. Some syllabi use the words interchangeably, but the definition question expects the distinction.
Forgetting the unit conversion in I. A diameter in mm must be changed to m before d⁴ is computed; otherwise the error is huge.

quiz.q: Define a strut and a column.
quiz.a: A strut is any member in axial compression, at any angle. A column is a vertical compression member.

quiz.q: Name three ideal end conditions for a column.
quiz.a: Both ends pinned; both ends fixed; one end fixed and one end free. Other valid answers are one fixed and one pinned, and both ends fixed but free to move sideways.

quiz.q: Why can a long column fail at a load much lower than the crushing load of its material?
quiz.a: A small initial curve or eccentricity gives the axial push a lever arm. Bending increases deflection, and deflection increases bending. At the critical load the sideways deflection grows without limit, so buckling occurs before the material crushes.

quiz.q: A column section has area A = 5000 mm² and least second moment I_min = 1.2 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Find its least radius of gyration.
Why is the least second moment of area used for buckling, not the largest?
quiz.a: The column can bend in any direction. It takes the path of least resistance, which is the axis with the smallest I. That axis gives the smallest r and the lowest buckling load, so it governs the design.

quiz.q: A rod is used once as a tie and once as a strut. Which use needs a buckling check, and why?
quiz.a: The strut needs the check because it is in compression and can bow sideways. The tie is in tension, and tension pulls it straight, so buckling does not occur.

quiz.q: If both ends of a column are changed from pinned to fixed, does the buckling load rise or fall? Explain in words.
quiz.a: It rises. Fixed ends stop rotation, so the buckled shape is forced into a shorter effective length. A shorter effective length gives a higher Euler buckling load.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, steel and concrete design codes replace the single Euler curve with column curves that allow for initial crookedness, residual stress and imperfections. Search for effective length, slenderness ratio, Perry-Robertson formula and code column curves. In buildings, the sway case is important because frames can move sideways, as in a portal frame under wind. In machine design, the same stability check appears in press rams, hydraulic cylinders and connecting rods.
